{{Short description|American theoretical physicist}}
'''David Alan Huse''' (born May 16, 1958) is an American [[theoretical physicist]], specializing in [[Statistical mechanics|statistical physics]] and [[condensed matter physics]].<ref name=NAS>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/david-a-huse-dewlxi/|title=David A. Huse|website=Member Directory, National Academy of Sciences (nasonline.org)}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://phy.princeton.edu/people/david-huse|title=David Huse &#124; Department of Physics|website=Princeton University}}</ref> Huse is known for his expertise in the fields of statistical physics and quantum many-body physics. He has  contributions to topics such as [[phase transition]]s, [[spin glass]]es and [[magnetic ordering]] in materials. His current research interests include ultracold atomic systems and non-equilibrium physics, and explore phenomena as quantum thermalization and many body localization.<ref>{{cite web|author=Meyer-Streng, Olivia|url=https://www.mpq.mpg.de/5415138/17_02_09|title=Professor David Huse elected MPQ "Distinguished Scholar"|date=February 9, 2017|website=Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics}}</ref>

==Biography==
After graduating from [[Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School]], Huse matriculated at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]], where he graduated in 1979 with a B.S. in physics.<ref name=APS/> He received in 1983 his Ph.D. from [[Cornell University]] with a thesis<ref>{{cite web|url=https://catalog.library.cornell.edu/catalog/70953|title=''Domain walls and the melting of commensurate phases'' by David Alan Huse, — thesis information, Cornell University Library Catalog|website=Cornell University}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=enRZAAAAYAAJ|title = Domain Walls and the Melting of Commensurate Phases|last1 = Huse|first1 = David Alan|year = 1983|publisher=Cornell University}}</ref> supervised by [[Michael E. Fisher]]. From 1983 to 1996, Huse worked in [[Bell Laboratories]] in Murray Hill. In 1996, he was appointed a professor in the physics department of [[Princeton University]].<ref name=APS>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Huse&first_nm=David&year=2022|title=2022 Lars Onsager Prize Recipient, David A. Huse|website=American Physical Society (APS)}}</ref> At the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], he has been appointed to positions for the autumn of 2010, and for the academic years 2015–2016, 2019–2020, and 2021–2022.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/david-huse|title=David A. Huse|website=Scholars, Institute for Advanced Study|date=9 December 2019}}</ref>

He was elected in 2010 a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Professor David Huse|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/david-huse}}</ref> in 2013 a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]],<ref>{{cite web|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science|title=Historic Fellows|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic}} (Search on "Huse".)</ref> and in 2017 a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=NAS/> In 2022 he received the [[Lars Onsager Prize]] with [[Boris Altshuler]] and [[Igor Aleiner]] for ""foundational work on many-body localization, its associated phase transition, and implications for thermalization and ergodicity."<ref name=APS/>

In 1982 he married Julia Smith. They have two sons.
